world_behind.title: What holds a city up
world_behind.text: The chapter opens by removing supports rather than by attacking walls. Bread, water, soldiers, judges, prophets, craftsmen, and speakers are listed as the things a society stands on, and the judgment is simply their absence. Isaiah does not describe an invasion here. He describes a vacancy.

world_behind.title: Ranks a Judean would recognize
world_behind.text: Captain of fifty, counselor, cunning artificer, eloquent orator: these are functions in a real administration, from the army's mid-level officer to the metalworker to the man who can speak in an assembly. Removing the list removes the state's ability to defend, decide, build, and persuade, in that order.

world_behind.title: Nobody will take the job
world_behind.text: Verses 6 and 7 show a man drafted as ruler because he still owns a cloak, and refusing on the grounds that he has no bread or clothing either. Leadership has become a liability rather than a prize. That is a specific kind of collapse, and it is worse than tyranny in the sense that no one is left who wants the office.

world_behind.title: Grinding faces
world_behind.text: The image in verse 15 is a millstone applied to people. Israel's law protected gleaners, debtors, and day laborers in detail, so this is not a general complaint about inequality; it is an accusation that specific legal duties toward the poor were being converted into profit.

world_behind.title: The wardrobe list
world_behind.text: Twenty-one items of clothing and jewelry are named in verses 18 through 23, some of them so specialized that their exact sense is uncertain now. Crisping-pins were probably curling tools, cauls a kind of net for the hair, tablets small scent boxes. The obscurity is part of the point: a whole industry of self-presentation, itemized and then removed.

world_behind.title: A colony reading about a wealthy capital
world_behind.text: Nephi's people had no daughters of Zion with tinkling ornaments and no captains of fifty. He copied the chapter anyway, immediately after the one about height, and the pairing suggests he read this as the working out of that principle rather than as news about Jerusalem.

words.text: Not a period but a person: an elder, one of the older men whose judgment carried weight in the gate. The word returns in verse 5, where "the child shall behave himself proudly against the ancient" (v. 5), and again in verse 14 where the ancients are put on trial. Isaiah removes the elders, then shows the young insulting them, then has God prosecute them. The same office appears three times in three conditions.

cites.quote: the child shall behave himself proudly against the ancient

spans.text: the child shall behave himself proudly against the ancient

words.text: A skilled maker, and the modifier matters: "the cunning artificer" (v. 3), where cunning means expert rather than sly. Craft knowledge is listed alongside military and legal skill as a pillar of the society. A people who lose their makers lose more than decoration, which the record's own writers understood, since they had a family tradition of fine workmanship.

Low, of no standing, the opposite of honorable in the same clause. The word measures social position rather than character. Isaiah's picture of disorder is not that bad people rise but that the ordering itself inverts, and he states it in the flattest available terms: child against elder, base against honorable.

The older sense is to uncover, to strip a covering off. Paired with the scab on the crown of the head, it makes a single point twice: what was arranged to be looked at will be exposed instead. The chapter's whole second half turns on that reversal, and this verb is where it starts.

Finery, showy splendor, with no reference to courage. The bravery of the tinkling ornaments is their glitter, and the word's older sense lets the verse name the display rather than the objects. What God takes away in verse 18 is not jewelry as such but the effect it was bought for.

phrases.text: The KJV repeats one noun: "the stay and the staff, the whole stay of bread" (Isa. 3:1). This reading distributes the pair, giving bread the staff and water the stay. The result matches the older idiom, in which God breaks "the staff of your bread" (Lev. 26:26) as a famine sentence, and it turns a repetition into a balanced line of two supports for two necessities.

phrases.term: let not this ruin come under thy hand
phrases.text: A single inserted negative flips the sentence. In the KJV the brother is drafted with the words "let this ruin be under thy hand" (Isa. 3:6), a request to take charge of the wreckage. Here the man is asked to rule and told to keep the ruin off his hands, which is an impossible commission, and it explains the oath of refusal in the very next verse.

The KJV says the people "hide it not" (Isa. 3:9), which reads as brazenness: they sin openly and are not ashamed. This reading says they are unable to. The difference relocates the failure from attitude to condition, and it agrees with the first half of the verse, where the face testifies whether its owner wants it to or not.

phrases.term: Say unto the righteous that it is well with them
phrases.text: The KJV promises a future in the singular: "it shall be well with him" (Isa. 3:10). Here it is present and plural. Between two verses of collapse, the righteous are told that things are well now, in the middle of the ruin rather than after it, which is a harder claim and a more useful one to a people surrounded by consequences they did not cause.

phrases.term: Wo unto the wicked, for they shall perish
phrases.text: The counterpart verdict is sharpened the same way. The KJV's "it shall be ill with him" (Isa. 3:11) is a mild phrase for a hard fate; this reading says perish. Read with verse 10, the pair becomes a clean two-sided sentence, present comfort against future ruin, with nothing left vague on either side.

phrases.term: eaten up the vineyard and the spoil of the poor
phrases.text: The KJV separates the charges with a semicolon: the vineyard is eaten, and the spoil of the poor is in your houses. This version runs them into one act, so what was consumed includes what was taken. The vineyard image is Isaiah's own and he will spend a whole chapter on it two chapters later, where the vineyard turns out to be the house of Israel.

phrases.term: What mean ye? Ye beat my people to pieces
phrases.text: The KJV asks one long question. This reading breaks it in two: a short demand for an explanation, then a flat statement of what they did. Nothing is added and nothing is removed, but the sentence now has a pause in it where the accused might have answered. The accusation lands after the silence.

verses.label: v. 1–3
verses.title: The supports removed, one by one
verses.text: Fourteen items in three verses, beginning with bread and water and ending with the man who can make a speech. The list has no verbs in it after the first, which gives it the feel of an inventory being crossed off. Judgment here is subtraction, and what is subtracted is competence.

verses.label: v. 4–7
verses.title: Children in charge, and no volunteers
verses.text: Princes who are children, neighbors oppressing neighbors, and then the small scene that makes it concrete: a man is nominated because he owns clothing and swears his way out of it. "I will not be a healer" (v. 7) is the refusal of a whole class to take responsibility, spoken by one man in a doorway.

cites.quote: I will not be a healer

spans.text: I will not be a healer

verses.label: v. 8–9
verses.title: The face gives it away
verses.text: The accusation moves from conduct to appearance. Their words and their doings provoked God, and now "the show of their countenance doth witness against them" (v. 9). Something has settled into the face that the person cannot arrange, and the comparison offered is Sodom, a city whose name had become shorthand for sin that no longer bothers to hide.

cites.quote: the show of their countenance doth witness against them

spans.text: the show of their countenance doth witness against them

verses.label: v. 10–11
verses.title: Two sentences, plainly stated
verses.text: The chapter stops describing and issues verdicts: well with the righteous, perishing for the wicked, each getting exactly what their own hands produced. The pair sits in the middle of the chapter without transition on either side, which is a way of saying that all the collapse around them does not change the arithmetic.

verses.label: v. 14–15
verses.title: The trial of the leaders
verses.text: God takes the posture of a prosecutor, standing up to plead and entering into judgment, and the defendants are the elders and princes. The charge is economic and the language is physical: eaten the vineyard, beaten people to pieces, ground the faces of the poor. Amos accused his own generation of panting "after the dust of the earth on the head of the poor" (Amos 2:7), which is the same picture from the other kingdom.

verses.label: v. 16–23
verses.title: The inventory of ornaments
verses.text: The daughters of Zion are described in motion first, necks stretched, eyes wandering, feet tinkling, and only then itemized. Twenty-one articles are listed without comment. The catalogue's length is the argument: an economy of appearance detailed at such length that its removal in verse 24 takes only one sentence.

verses.label: v. 24–26
verses.title: Instead of, instead of
verses.text: Five substitutions in a single verse, each trading a refinement for its opposite, and the last is the hardest: "burning instead of beauty" (v. 24). Then the men fall and the city sits on the ground. The chapter ends with a personified Jerusalem in the posture of a mourner, which is where the ornaments were supposed to prevent her from ever being seen.

chapter.title: Judgment by removal
chapter.text: Almost nothing in this chapter is actively destroyed until the last two verses. Supports are taken away, leaders are absent, ornaments are removed, and the society collapses inward. It is a portrait of what a place looks like when what held it up is withdrawn, and it is more disturbing than a battle scene for exactly that reason.

chapter.title: The chapter continues the previous one's argument
chapter.text: Chapter 12 brought down everything high; this one shows the aftermath at street level. The daughters of Zion are called haughty using the same vocabulary that condemned the lofty looks of men, and Nephi copied the two chapters in order without comment between them.

chapter.title: The variants sharpen verdicts and fix difficulties
chapter.text: The added negative in verse 6 makes a strange draft notice coherent, the inability to hide in verse 9 replaces mere shamelessness, and the two verdicts in verses 10 and 11 are moved into present tense and plain outcome. The pattern matches what the block does elsewhere: the reading is more explicit than its source.

chapter.title: The poor are the measure
chapter.text: The trial in verses 14 and 15 does not charge idolatry or foreign alliance, though Isaiah accuses Judah of both in neighboring chapters. It charges what was done to the poor. In a chapter about the loss of leadership, the specific failure named is the use of office to take from people who could not resist.

chapter.title: A long list against a short sentence
chapter.text: Twenty-one ornaments take six verses; their removal takes half of one. The imbalance is the chapter's most effective device, and it is available to any reader who counts. Whatever took years to accumulate is described as going in a single clause.

chapter.title: The women's section is not a separate subject
chapter.text: It follows the trial of the elders directly, and it uses the same logic: something arranged for display is exposed instead. Reading verses 16 through 24 as an attack on women misses that the men have already been through the same treatment in verses 1 through 15, in their own currency of office and rank.

chapter.title: Placed early in the block for a reason
chapter.text: Nephi's colony was new, small, and about to become prosperous. Two chapters into his Isaiah selection he has copied a description of a society that had everything this one lacked and lost all of it from the inside. Nothing in the chapter needs adapting to be useful.

applications.title: Name your supports
applications.text: Isaiah lists what a society stands on before describing its fall. Write the five things your own life currently stands on, in order, and ask which of them you have been treating as permanent. The exercise is not morbid; it is how you find out what you have been quietly trusting.

applications.title: Take the office nobody wants
applications.text: The scene turns on a man who had a cloak and would not serve. Look for the responsibility in your family, ward, or workplace that is going begging, and take one piece of it this month without waiting to feel qualified.

applications.title: Check the countenance
applications.text: The verse claims a face eventually reports what a life is doing. Ask someone who knows you well what your face has been saying lately. It is an uncomfortable question and a fast diagnostic.

applications.title: Audit one transaction against the poor
applications.text: The charge is specific: eating the vineyard and the spoil together. Look at one place where your gain depends on somebody's weak position, a price, a wage, a delay, and change the term you would not want read out in court.

applications.title: Count what you have accumulated for display
applications.text: Make the list Isaiah makes, in your own categories, and let it be as long as it honestly is. Then ask what it would cost you if the whole list went, and whether the answer is money or identity.

applications.title: Drop the future clause
applications.text: Try saying the verse's verdict over your own week in the tense it uses, with nothing added about how it will get better later. Notice what in you reaches for the postponement, and whether the reaching is humility or unbelief.

questions.text: Where in my life have I let unqualified things rule because the qualified ones were removed or ignored?
What responsibility have I sworn my way out of, and what was the honest reason?
If my face testifies, what is it currently testifying?
Who leads me, and are they causing me to err in ways I have decided not to examine?
Whose face have I ground, in small ways, to make my own situation easier?
If beauty in my life were traded for its opposite tomorrow, what would remain that I actually built?
